title: product-service soft-deletes a product without checking for active inventory reservations, while inventory-service refuses to delete an in-use inventory row
actual: InventoryServiceImpl.delete() refuses to delete an inventory row that has PENDING or COMMITTED reservations (ErrorCode.INVENTORY_IN_USE). The symmetric guard does not exist on the other side of the relationship: ProductServiceImpl.delete() soft-deletes the product unconditionally, so a product can be removed from the catalogue while stock for it is reserved or committed. The inventory row survives with a reference to a soft-deleted product.
expected: A product with live reservations cannot be removed from the catalogue, or the inventory row is released/compensated as part of the deletion.
trigger: An administrator deletes a product that a customer is currently checking out.
root_cause: The guard lives only on the inventory side, and inventory-service has no visibility of the product catalogue - the check would have to be an HTTP call, which the product-service does not make.
consequences: An orphaned inventory row for a deleted product; the checkout can still commit a reservation for a product that no longer exists; the reserved stock is never returned to the sellable pool.
remediation: Add a reference check to the product delete path (the same internal client pattern media-service already uses via MediaReferenceChecker / ProductMediaReferenceChecker), and make the check fail-safe: treat an unavailable reference service as 'referenced' so a delete is not performed on incomplete data.
regression_test: Integration test: deleting a product that has an active reservation must be rejected; deleting one with none must succeed.

title: product-service soft-deletes a variant with a hard-coded 'system' actor and without a stock check
actual: ProductVariantServiceImpl.delete() calls variant.markDeleted("system") - the actor is a literal, not the resolved principal, so a destructive administrative change is attributed to a pseudo-actor regardless of who performed it. It also performs no stock check, unlike the product delete path's sibling in inventory-service.
expected: The resolved actor is recorded, and a variant with live stock is not silently removed.
trigger: An administrator deletes a product variant.
root_cause: The variant delete path was written separately from the product/brand/category delete paths and hard-codes the actor.
consequences: The audit trail cannot attribute a variant deletion. Combined with F-049 (two conventions across the fleet) the soft-delete attribution is inconsistent in three different ways.
remediation: Resolve the actor through the same AuditorAware-based helper the fleet should share (see F-049), and add a stock-reference check.
regression_test: Unit test: the deleted variant records the authenticated actor.

title: The media upload path amplifies memory to hundreds of megabytes for a single maximum-size image
actual: The upload path holds, simultaneously: the raw source bytes (file.getBytes(), up to shop.media.max-upload-bytes), a decoded BufferedImage (width x height x 4 bytes - the guard permits up to 8192 x 8192, i.e. 268 MB for one image), and the encoded bytes of every rendered variant (up to six byte arrays). The source is also parsed twice: once by ImageMetadataReader for the EXIF/GPS inspection and once by ImageIO, and the image is decoded a second time by ImageIO.read after the dimension probe. The dimension guard limits width and height but the pixel-count guard is width*height <= 8192*8192, which is exactly the 268 MB case.
expected: The upload path must bound its peak heap so a single upload cannot exhaust the service's heap, and must not decode the same image twice.
trigger: An administrator uploads a large (but permitted) image.
root_cause: The size guard is expressed in source bytes and in pixel dimensions, but not in the memory the decoder will actually allocate; the header probe and the full decode are two separate passes over the same bytes.
consequences: A single upload can allocate several hundred megabytes of heap. Concurrent uploads multiply that, and the result is a heap-exhaustion outage of media-service rather than a rejected upload. The objective's 'memory and CPU behaviour for large uploads' requirement is not met.
remediation: Express the guard in decoded-memory terms (width x height x 4 plus the source size must fit a configured budget), decode once (reuse the ImageReader stream for both the dimension probe and the decode), and stream the source to the digest instead of materialising it twice.
regression_test: Performance test: upload an image at the configured maximum and assert the peak heap stays inside the configured budget; a unit test asserts that an image whose decoded size exceeds the budget is rejected before any large allocation.

title: Deleting a media asset does not check whether a live product still references it
actual: media-service already has the reference checker (ProductMediaReferenceChecker) and it is deliberately fail-safe - an unavailable reference service is treated as REFERENCED so the purge job skips the media. The DELETE endpoint path does NOT use it: MediaLifecycleServiceImpl.softDelete() soft-deletes unconditionally, so an administrator can remove a media asset that a live product still points at, leaving the product with a dangling image reference.
expected: Deleting a referenced media asset is refused (or the references are cleared first), with the same fail-safe posture the purge job uses.
trigger: An administrator deletes a media asset used by a live product.
root_cause: The reference check was wired into the background purge path but not into the interactive delete path.
consequences: A live product loses its image; the reference count and the catalogue disagree.
remediation: Apply the existing reference checker in the delete path, reusing the fail-safe semantics already implemented.
regression_test: Integration test: deleting a referenced media asset must be refused; deleting an unreferenced one must succeed.

title: The 'six WebP variants' claim is inaccurate: the renderer produces six objects for a JPEG/PNG upload, but only three of them are WebP
actual: VariantRenderer.render() walks the three variants (original, display, thumb) and, for each, emits the source format plus a WebP copy - unless the source format is already WebP. A JPEG upload therefore yields six objects (original.jpg, original.webp, display.jpg, display.webp, thumb.jpg, thumb.webp) of which THREE are WebP; a WebP upload yields three objects, all WebP.
expected: The documentation states the actual number of WebP variants per upload.
trigger: Any statement about how many WebP variants the platform produces.
root_cause: The documented count conflated 'variants' with 'WebP variants'.
consequences: A capacity or storage estimate based on the claim is wrong by a factor of two; an operator verifying the claim by counting WebP objects finds three, not six.
remediation: Correct the claim to 'three variants (original, display, thumb), each stored in the source format and in WebP - six objects for a JPEG or PNG upload, three for a WebP upload'.
regression_test: Integration test asserting the rendered object count per source format.

title: Hiding the only visible rating of a product crashed the moderation transaction - the administrator could not remove the review
actual: RatingEventService.record() reads the aggregate with findAggregateByProductId, whose JPQL averages over hidden = false AND deleted = false. When the last visible rating of a product is hidden, PostgreSQL returns a NULL average. toBigDecimal() called String.valueOf(raw), which for a null Object returns the literal string "null" (not null), and new BigDecimal("null") throws NumberFormatException. The exception propagated out of record(), inside the hide transaction, so the whole hide rolled back and the API answered 500. A moderator therefore could not remove the only review of a product - exactly the situation moderation exists for, and a dead end that leaves an abusive review visible.
expected: Hiding the last visible rating succeeds and reports an average of zero.
trigger: An administrator hides a rating when it is the only visible rating for its product.
root_cause: A NULL aggregate value was passed to a numeric parser that handled the 'not a BigDecimal' case but not the 'null' case.
consequences: The moderation endpoint fails with a 500 for a legitimate and important operation; the abusive review stays visible and the operator has no other route.
remediation: toBigDecimal() now maps a null aggregate to BigDecimal.ZERO.
regression_test: rating-service: RatingEventServiceTest.record_withNullAggregateAverage_writesZeroAverageInsteadOfFailing asserts the event is written with avgRating 0.00 and ratingCount 0.
verification_evidence: rating-service module green with the new regression test.

title: Remote calls are made inside database transactions in three more services (product media check, rating eligibility, order cancel)
actual: ProductServiceImpl.create/update call assertMediaExists -> mediaHeadClient.exists() inside the @Transactional method. RatingServiceImpl.submit calls eligibilityClient.isEligible() inside its @Transactional method. OrderServiceImpl.cancelOrder (already recorded as F-027) performs the inventory, promotion and payment calls inside its @Transactional method. Each holds a pooled DB connection and an open transaction for the duration of a remote round-trip (3-5 second timeouts).
expected: Remote calls run outside the transaction; the local state change commits in a short transaction - the shape the checkout saga already uses deliberately.
trigger: Any slowdown of media-service, order-service or the payment provider.
root_cause: The same pattern as F-027, repeated in three services that were written independently.
consequences: A degraded downstream holds DB connections and transactions open. With Hikari maximum-pool-size=20 a burst of concurrent requests against a slow dependency can exhaust the pool and stall unrelated requests on the same service.
remediation: Move the remote verification out of the transaction: perform it first, then open the short transaction for the write. Where the remote result must be authoritative (the rating eligibility check), fail the request rather than holding the transaction open.
regression_test: Concurrency test: hold the downstream at 2s per call and assert the service's connection pool is not exhausted.
